title: Fractional batch slicing and grace-period experiments
body:
Purpose:
This doc captures a set of exploratory experiments for two related ideas we haven't tried at scale: (1) fractional-batch-slicing — allowing a partially-filled batch to be split across multiple inference workers (or CPU pre/post pipelines) so work begins earlier but still leverages collective kernel work; and (2) a short, configurable grace period for hot-path requests that biases slightly toward latency while still allowing some batching to occur. The goal is to understand tradeoffs in tail latency, throughput, and fairness between tenants/priority classes when we mix these techniques into the continuous batching scheduler.

Motivation / why different from prior runs:
- Existing experiments (many linked in the parent folder) focus on flush timeouts, priority demotion, and sampler heuristics. Fractional slicing changes the unit of execution: instead of waiting for a batch to reach N requests before dispatching to a device, we can dispatch a fraction (e.g. 50%) of the batch earlier and continue filling the rest while the device is running.
- Grace period is different from a hard timeout: it's a tiny, tunable window (100-500us) used for requests that are likely to be alone or low-arrival; it gives them a better latency without blowing up throughput.

Hypotheses (tested):
H1: Fractional slicing reduces P99 latency under mixed bursty workloads by up to 15% because long-waiting requests get started earlier.
H2: Grace period of 200-300us reduces P95 by ~10% for low QPS customers at acceptable throughput loss (~<3%).
H3: Combined approach improves fairness across priority cohorts (measured as inter-quantile gap between high/low priority P95) but may increase kernel overhead leading to slight throughput drop on small models.

Experiment matrix (high-level):
- Workloads: steady 500qps, bursty 2k qps with spikes, low-qps 20 qps noisy background.
- Models: small (7B fp16), med (13B int8-ish), large (70B quantized).
- Variables: fractional slice ratios (0.25, 0.5, 0.75), grace windows (0us, 100us, 200us, 500us), priority weightings (equal, 2x high-priority), sampler on/off.
- Metrics: P50/P90/P95/P99 latency (end-to-end), tail token latency (first-token vs final-token), tokens/sec, GPU utilization, kernel-launch counts per-second, fairness delta (P95_high - P95_low), cost-estimate delta (approx CPU+GPU).

Microbench harness and how we ran it:
- Bench runner: bench/runner v0.12.1 (internal) with reproducible seeds, 30m runs.
- Cluster: 4x A100-80G hosts for model sizes up to 70B; 2x A500 for small experiments.
- Scheduler build: feature branch "fractional-slice-experiment" (#8021).
- Command (example):
  ./bench-runner --config exp-2025-11-fractional.yaml --duration 1800 --seeds 3 --trace --outdir /bench/exp-2025-11-fractional/run-01
- Key config snippet used (textual):
  scheduler: 
    continuous_batching: true
    fractional_slice: {enabled: true, slice_ratio: 0.5, max_slices: 4}
    grace_period_us: 200
    sampling: {enabled: true, policy: age_weighted}

Representative results (selected):
- Workload: bursty 2k qps, model: 13B int8, batch_target: 64
  baseline (no fractional, no grace): P50=38ms, P95=142ms, P99=312ms, tokens/s=98k, kernel_launches/s=153
  fractional=0.5, grace=200us: P50=34ms, P95=128ms, P99=265ms, tokens/s=96.5k, kernel_launches/s=174
  fractional=0.25, grace=100us: P50=36ms, P95=136ms, P99=290ms, tokens/s=97k, kernel_launches/s=168
  notes: fractional reduced P99 considerably; kernel launches increased ~14% raising CPU & kernel setup overhead but still net throughput ~-1.5%.

- Workload: low-qps steady 20qps, model: 7B fp16, batch_target: 32
  baseline: P50=22ms, P95=190ms, P99=510ms, tokens/s=3.9k
  grace=300us only: P50=20ms, P95=150ms, P99=420ms, tokens/s=3.8k
  fractional disabled + grace 300us: big wins for P95 without throttle to throughput.

- Workload: steady 500qps mixed priorities, model: 70B quantized, batch_target: 128
  baseline: P95_high=110ms, P95_low=210ms (fairness delta=100ms)
  fractional=0.5 + grace=200us: P95_high=105ms, P95_low=165ms (delta=60ms)
  observation: fairness delta shrank, but GPU occupancy dip by ~3% and kernel launches up 22% (expensive on large model).

Profiling observations (from perf traces & simple flamegraphs):
- Kernel launch overhead: fractional slicing increases the number of kernel setups per unit time because we call forward() more often on partially-filled batches. On large models this dominates.
- Copy & prep overhead: smaller slices had disproportionate CPU/host->device memcpy overhead. We saw memcpy time as a larger fraction of wall time for slice_ratio <=0.25.
- Queue head blocking: grace period reduces head-of-queue blocking events; the scheduler logs show fewer demotions/priority flips and fewer preemptions for high-priority traffic.
- Memory fragmentation: we observed transient GPU memory fragmentation when mixing many small slices and multi-tenant pools; coalescing mem allocs helped.

Sample scheduler log excerpt (timestamps simplified):
  [2025-11-20T13:12:22.117Z] accept req id=rhd-1024 pri=high -> queued slot(12)
  [2025-11-20T13:12:22.119Z] slice_created batch=89 slice=1/2 size=32 scheduled->device A
  [2025-11-20T13:12:22.119Z] accept req id=rhd-1025 pri=low -> queued slot(13)
  [2025-11-20T13:12:22.119Z] slice_created batch=89 slice=2/2 size=32 scheduled->device A
  [2025-11-20T13:12:22.219Z] device A kernel_complete batch=89 tokens=2048
  notes: you can see two slices launched ~100us apart; the earlier start improved P50 for the first requests in that batch.

Risk and tradeoffs summary:
- Pros: reduced tail for mixed traffic, improved fairness, configurable knobs that can be tuned per-plane (dedicated vs shared). Works especially well for mid-size models (10–30B) where kernel overhead is moderate.
- Cons: more kernel launches -> more CPU work and memcpy; potential throughput regression on the largest models; memory fragmentation; increased complexity in accounting/metrics (we need to attribute tokens to slices).

Practical mitigations tried during runs:
- Coalesce memcpy: reuse pinned buffers for small slices to reduce memcpy/syscall overhead. Reduced CPU overhead by ~8%.
- Adaptive slice sizing: auto-decrease slice_count if kernel_launch_rate > threshold. Helped keep throughput stable.
- Grace period backoff: dynamically shrink grace window under heavy load. Stops grace from hurting throughput in peaks.

Open questions / next experiments:
1) Can we move slice coalescing deeper into the device runtime so multiple partial kernels are fused (reduce kernel_launch count)? Requires device runtime work (CUDA graph-like).
2) Interaction with KV-cache for chats: when we start a partial forward early, does KV cache coherence cause rework when rest of batch arrives? Need a chat-focused test.
3) Cost model: quantify CPU cost in $/1M tokens for different slice ratios (we have rough estimates but need billing-sim).
4) Long-running stability test: run 72h with multi-tenant mix to observe fragmentation and scheduler fairness drift.
5) Explore non-uniform slice ratios (e.g., start with 25% then 75%) vs fixed slices.

Action items (owners):
- Priya: run 72h stability with 70B quantized, fractional=0.5, grace=200us (ticket -> RI-2849).
- Ben: prototype device-side coalescer sketch (RFC) and perf estimate.
- Evan: add slice-attribution metrics to observability (trace spans + cost counters).
- Aisha (me): write a short proposal for config defaults per deployment mode: hosted/dedicated/private.

Appendix: short checklist to reproduce
- checkout: git checkout -b fractional-slice-experiment origin/feature/fractional-slice
- build: make -C runtime all && docker build -t rr/runtime:frac .
- upload config to bench: cp exp-2025-11-fractional.yaml /bench/configs/
- run: ./bench-runner --config exp-2025-11-fractional.yaml --duration 3600 --trace
- collect traces: /bench/exp-2025-11-fractional/run-*/trace-*.pstat -> profiler viewer

Notes to reviewers:
- This is exploratory; numbers are noisy across seeds. Use the linked artifact console for raw CSVs (we ran 3 seeds per cell).
- Please comment on whether fractional slicing belongs behind an experimental feature flag per-customer (my leaning: yes, default off for Private and Dedicated; small-hosted pools maybe opt-in).

End of notes.
